entries.title: How a machine digs a tunnel
entries.answer: One way to dig a tunnel is with a round machine that cuts through earth or rock as it advances. Its head breaks the material into small pieces. Belts, pipes or special carts remove the pieces. The fresh tunnel often needs support, so workers or equipment place walls or pipes behind the cutter as it moves. Machines for wet, loose ground can also press against the digging face to keep soil and water from rushing in.
facts: Builders choose different tools for hard rock and for soft wet soil.

questions.text: What moves huge pieces of ground over longer times?
What kind of travel uses large tunnels beneath some cities?

entries.title: How a suspension bridge hangs from cables
entries.answer: On a suspension bridge, smaller vertical lines hang the roadway from large curved cables. Towers support the high points of those cables. Strong connections in the ground hold the cables at the ends, otherwise the weight of the roadway would pull them inward. The towers carry much of the load down to their foundations. This arrangement lets builders cross a wide area without planting a row of supports in the middle of rivers or shipping lanes.
facts: The cables mainly experience pulling forces rather than being squeezed.

questions.text: How can a curved bridge carry a load without hanging from cables?
How can triangles keep a bridge from bending too much?
What makes the roadway weigh anything in the first place?

entries.title: How a traffic light can detect a waiting car
entries.answer: Some traffic lights follow a schedule, while others can change when a vehicle is waiting. One kind of detector uses wire arranged in a loop under the road. Electricity in the loop produces a magnetic field, and a large metal vehicle above it changes the electrical behavior a little. The detector sends a message to the traffic signal’s controller. A signal can also detect vehicles using a camera or equipment that sends radio waves.
facts: A detector can tell a signal that a car is in a lane without needing to know who is driving.

questions.text: What can electric current do in a loop of wire?
How can a different road design guide traffic without signals?
How can a measurement become a message to a computer?

entries.title: How an arch bridge carries weight
entries.answer: An arch bridge uses a curved shape to carry loads toward the ground at each end. The stones in a traditional arch lean on one another, so the weight mainly squeezes them together. The curve also pushes outward at both ends. Strong supports on those sides have to keep the feet of the arch from spreading. Builders once used this shape to carry roads and water channels over valleys, often placing many arches in a row.
facts: Stone handles squeezing much better than being pulled apart.

questions.text: What ancient water system used rows of arches?
Which bridge supports its road by hanging it from cables?
Why do other bridges use straight bars instead of curved stones?

entries.title: How an elevator goes up and down
entries.answer: Many elevators hang the car from strong ropes or belts over a powered wheel. A counterweight hangs on the opposite side and helps balance the car’s weight. That way the motor does not need to lift the full weight of the car by itself. Guide rails keep the car moving along the same path. The machine can stop the car level with a floor, and modern elevators have brakes and other protective systems.
facts: Some elevators are raised by a hydraulic piston instead of a moving rope and counterweight.

questions.text: How can a piston lift a load from below?
How can a turning wheel guide a lifting rope?
How does a moving staircase carry people continuously between levels?

entries.title: How canal locks raise and lower boats
entries.answer: A lock is a short section of water with gates at both ends. A boat enters while the lock’s water matches the level outside the open gate. Once inside, the gate shuts. Water flows in from the higher side or drains to the lower side, and the floating boat moves up or down with it. When the water matches the next part of the canal, the other gate can open and the boat moves on.
facts: A boat keeps floating throughout the change in height.

questions.text: Why can water stand at different heights on two sides of a dam?
What holds a heavy ship up as the lock fills?
How did Roman builders move water without pumping it uphill?

entries.title: How dams hold and release water
entries.answer: A dam is a barrier built across a valley or a river. Water gathers behind it in a reservoir. People can release water when fields or towns need it or send it through turbines to make electricity. During heavy rain, some dams hold back part of a flood for a short time. A spillway lets extra water go around or over the dam safely. Dams can also change where fish travel and where sediment collects.
facts: A reservoir can store water between wet and dry seasons.

questions.text: How does falling water make electricity at some dams?
How can boats get past a place where water stands at different heights?
What happens to bits of rock that flowing water can lift and carry?

entries.title: How drinking water gets cleaned
entries.answer: Water from a river or lake can carry dirt and tiny living things. A treatment plant can add substances that help tiny bits of dirt clump together. Heavy clumps settle, and the water then goes through filters that catch more particles. Disinfection uses methods such as chlorine or ultraviolet light to kill or inactivate many germs. The exact steps depend on the source and the quality of the water. Pipes carry the cleaned water to buildings.
facts: Very clear water can still contain things too small to see.

questions.text: How does treated water reach taps with enough pressure?
What happens to water after it goes down a sink?
How did water get to a river or lake first?

entries.title: How electricity gets to your home
entries.answer: Power plants and other sources make electricity in many places. The power grid links these sources to towns, cities and buildings. Thick wires carry power a long way, often at high voltage to reduce energy lost along the way. Along that route, transformers lower the voltage for smaller local wires and for use in homes. Grid operators try to match the supply of electricity with what people are using at each moment.
facts: A substation helps put power onto different lines or changes the voltage to serve a local area.

questions.text: What makes the current that can travel through power lines?
How can some buildings make part of their own electricity?
How does a closed path let a lamp use electrical energy?

entries.title: How escalator steps go flat at the top
entries.answer: An escalator runs a loop of steps around on a long chain. The visible steps ride upward or downward on wheels set in tracks. The tracks change their height relative to one another so the steps stay level where you stand but flatten together at the ends. After sliding under the landing, the steps loop around and travel back underneath. A second moving loop gives people a handrail that travels alongside them.
facts: An escalator and a moving walkway both use a returning loop hidden beneath the visible path.

questions.text: How does an elevator move a whole room between floors?
How can the wheels under a loaded step turn smoothly?
What parts can transfer power from a motor to a chain?

entries.title: How railway signals help keep trains apart
entries.answer: One way to manage a railway is to divide it into sections called blocks. Equipment can tell a signaling system whether a train is in a block. Signals then help the next driver or automatic controls know whether the route ahead is available. This matters because a heavy train needs a long distance to stop, so relying only on seeing another train could leave too little time. Railways use several ways to detect trains and share information.
facts: Some signal systems use equipment in the tracks to tell whether a train is present.

questions.text: What physical parts let trains take different paths?
Why is separation important on a city line with frequent trains?
How is separation also important for planes near airports?

entries.title: How trains change tracks without steering
entries.answer: Train wheels follow metal rails, so a driver cannot turn a train the way a driver steers a car. At a junction, two short, tapered rails can move a little sideways. In one position they guide the wheels along the main track. In the other they make a smooth path into the branching track. Signals help manage which trains can use that part of the railway. The track arrangement has to be ready before the first wheels reach it.
facts: The moving parts that guide the wheels are called switch points.

questions.text: Why does a subway system also need track junctions?
How did older trains get the power to turn the wheels that follow the rails?
Why do very fast trains usually run on specially designed tracks?

entries.title: What do the big numbers at the end of a runway mean?
entries.answer: A runway is a strip where an aircraft can take off and land. Large numbers at the ends usually describe the direction a plane faces as it goes along the strip. In the United States, the numbers usually come from the direction measured with a magnetic compass, rounded and shortened. The other end points nearly the opposite way. White lines down the middle can mark the center, and other markings can show where a landing area begins.
facts: At airports with several parallel runways, letters sometimes tell apart strips that have nearly the same direction.

questions.text: Why can a compass and a map show slightly different north directions?
Who helps different planes use the same runways without crossing paths?
What happens to the wings when a plane is getting ready to land?

entries.title: Where does rain on a street go?
entries.answer: After rain falls on a street, much of it cannot soak through the hard surface. Water runs along slopes and gutters to an opening or grate. Some drains send this water through pipes to a pond, stream or river. The rain can carry soil, trash or oil it picked up along the way. Unlike the water that leaves a sink, stormwater in many places goes through different pipes. Some older systems share pipes for both.
facts: Moving rainwater from hard surfaces is called runoff.

questions.text: How can a planted dip slow water on its way toward a drain?

entries.title: Where water goes after it runs down the drain
entries.answer: Water that leaves sinks or toilets can move through sewer pipes to a treatment plant. Screens catch big pieces of trash first. In tanks, some smaller solid pieces settle while other material floats and can be removed. In another stage, tiny living things help break down much of the waste still mixed into the water. Plants may remove more material and disinfect the water before returning it to a river or using it again.
facts: The settled mixture left from treatment is often called sludge.

questions.text: How is making river water safe to drink a separate job?

Why do rivers need oxygen for plants, animals and microbes?

entries.title: Why airports have traffic control towers
entries.answer: Many airports have tall towers where controllers can look out at the runways and paths between gates. They talk with pilots and help keep aircraft apart while airplanes land, take off or move on the ground. Other controllers watch displays and coordinate flights farther from an airport. Bad weather may mean only a few planes can use a runway at once. In that case, the controllers and the people planning traffic can change when planes arrive.
facts: Keeping aircraft apart is one of the controller’s most important jobs.

entries.title: Why bridge frames are full of triangles
entries.answer: A rectangular frame can lean sideways if its joints are free to turn. Add a diagonal bar, and you split the frame into two triangles. Three sides of fixed lengths hold one triangle shape, so they resist that sideways change. A truss bridge joins many triangles in a frame. When a car drives across it, some bars are squeezed and some are pulled. The bars spread the car’s load to the bridge’s supports.
facts: A truss needs strong joints as well as strong bars.

questions.text: How does another bridge shape carry loads mostly by squeezing?

Why can where you apply a force matter as much as the force itself?

entries.title: Why build a circle where roads meet?
entries.answer: A modern roundabout sends traffic around a small island so paths join in the same direction. The road bends as it leads toward the center, which helps drivers slow before entering the circle. Drivers can then move off along the road they need. Where an ordinary crossing allows several paths to cut across one another, a roundabout has fewer places where moving vehicles meet at right angles. The island’s shape helps guide cars, buses and trucks along useful paths.
facts: A roundabout is shaped to make drivers travel more slowly where paths join.

entries.title: Why some electrical problems turn the power off
entries.answer: A wire can heat up if more electric current passes through it than it was made to carry. A protective device called a circuit breaker can open the wire’s path automatically. Current then stops flowing along that path, cutting power to the parts it supplies. A fuse serves a similar purpose but uses a small piece of metal that melts to break the path. In either case, opening the circuit helps keep the wiring from overheating.
facts: A circuit breaker and a light switch both open a circuit, but the breaker can do it automatically when there is a problem.

questions.text: Why can lights elsewhere still work when one branch turns off?
Why does cutting a tiny gap stop the current?
What happens to energy after it makes one part of a wire warm?

entries.title: Why some gardens are planted lower than the ground
entries.answer: A rain garden looks like a shallow hollow planted with things that can handle occasional wet soil. Water rushing off a roof, road or path can spread out and slow down in the hollow. The slower water has more time to soak through the soil, where some loose bits and other materials can be removed. After the garden drains, the plants can keep growing. Rain gardens can reduce the stream of water reaching a storm drain.
facts: A rain garden holds water for a short time, rather than staying full all year.

Why can faster moving water pick up more loose soil?

entries.title: Why water towers are so tall
entries.answer: A water tower holds a tank high above the ground. Pumps fill the tank when they can, and gravity helps push its stored water down into the town’s pipes. Putting the water higher raises the pressure at a lower tap, much like lifting one end of a hose full of water can make it flow out of the other. The tank can help meet short periods of heavy use, such as when many showers are running together.
facts: A town may use more than one tank where the land has very different heights.
